title: Diagnostic evaluation of an EF1α RT-qPCR assay for RNA quality control in IPNV detection.
abstract: Reliable detection of infectious pancreatic necrosis virus (IPNV) by real-time RT-qPCR requires stable internal reference genes to control for variability in RNA quality, extraction efficiency, and reverse transcription. In salmonid diagnostics, the housekeeping gene elongation factor 1 alpha (EF1α) is widely used for this purpose; however, different RT-qPCR protocols targeting EF1α are often adopted without comparative evaluation of assay performance. In this study, we compared three RT-qPCR assays targeting EF1α (Moore, Bowers, and a newly designed assay, ELF4) using 53 field samples from three salmonid species (Salmo salar, Oncorhynchus mykiss, and O. kisutch). Differences in Ct dispersion were observed among assays, with the Bowers and ELF4 protocols showing significantly lower variability than the Moore assay. The ELF4 assay was subsequently validated as an endogenous sample control for diagnostic applications using two independent datasets: 500 pooled kidney-spleen samples collected during a confirmed IPNV outbreak in 2023 and 81 samples (47 survivors and 34 mortality cases) from a previously published experimental challenge. Across outbreak samples, ELF4 Ct values remained consistent, whereas IPNV VP1 Ct values showed wider dispersion, reflecting variability in viral RNA levels. A moderate positive correlation was observed between ELF4 and VP1 Ct values (Spearman's ρ = 0.40, p < 0.001), suggesting that sample-dependent variation in RNA quality may influence viral RNA detectability under field conditions. These results support the use of the ELF4 EF1α RT-qPCR assay as a robust endogenous sample control for IPNV detection. Incorporation of ELF4 into routine diagnostic workflows may improve RNA quality assessment and enhance the reliability of RT-qPCR-based surveillance in salmonid aquaculture.

title: Hemodynamic forces provide incremental predictive value for left ventricular remodeling after STEMI.
abstract: Purpose This study aimed to determine the prognostic significance of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-derived Hemodynamic forces (HDF) parameters for adverse left ventricular remodeling (ALVR) in patients following ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and to compare their predictive value with conventional risk markers. Methods 147 STEMI patients from two hospitals underwent CMR within 7 days and at 5 months post-percutaneous coronary intervetion (PCI). ALVR was defined as a ≥ 15% increase in left ventricular end-systolic volume. Baseline clinical, conventional CMR, strain, and HDF parameters were analyzed. Three multivariate logistic regression models were constructed: Model 1 (traditional parameters), Model 1 + strains, and Model 1 + HDF parameters, to assess incremental predictive value for ALVR. Results In the multivariable regression model incorporating traditional parameters, strain, and HDF parameters, infarct percentage (OR: 1.127, 95% CI: 1.048-1.213, P = 0.001) and systolic HDF impulse (OR: 0.757, 95% CI: 0.629-0.911, P = 0.003) remained independent predictors of ALVR. Adding systolic HDF impulse to LVEF and infarct percentage significantly increased the AUC from 0.745 to 0.799 (P < 0.001). In contrast, the inclusion of myocardial global circumferential strain (MyoGCS) did not provide incremental value. Consistent with these findings, the likelihood ratio test confirmed that adding systolic HDF impulse significantly improved model performance (P = 0.004), whereas adding MyoGCS did not (P = 0.310). Conclusion Systolic HDF impulse provides prognostic value beyond conventional markers, including infarct percentage and LVEF, supporting its potential utility for improving post-infarction risk stratification.

title: Reduced volume of neuromodulatory brainstem nuclei is associated with early hallucination-related vulnerability in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Early hallucination-related phenomena, including minor visual hallucinations (mVHs), are clinically relevant features of Parkinson's disease (PD), but their neuroanatomical substrates remain unclear. Brainstem nuclei supporting sensory gating, together with cholinergic and noradrenergic dysregulation, are proposed modulators of hallucinations. The objective of the present study was to test whether PD participants with early hallucination-related phenomena show reduced volumes of brainstem nuclei with cholinergic and noradrenergic relevance, using cross-sectional analysis of baseline structural MRI, clinical, and neuropsychological data from 641 PD participants in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). Participants scoring ≥1 at screening, baseline, or during the first nine months of follow-up were categorized as PD-mVHs + , whereas those who consistently scored 0 throughout the first year were categorized as PD-mVHs - . Histology-informed probabilistic atlases were used to segment brainstem, subcortical, and cortical regions. Analyses of covariance (ANCOVAs) compared regional volumes across groups, with group and sex as fixed factors, the group × sex interaction, and age, education, standardized estimated intracranial volume (eTIV), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score, and disease duration as continuous covariates. Hierarchical logistic regression tested whether brainstem volumes added explanatory value for hallucination-related status beyond clinical, neuropsychological, and other volumetric predictors. PD-mVHs + participants showed reduced left locus coeruleus (LC) and left laterodorsal tegmental nucleus (LDTg) volumes, with no significant differences in pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus or dorsal raphe nuclei. After covariate adjustment, the left LDTg effect survived both Bonferroni and false discovery rate (FDR) correction, whereas the left LC effect survived FDR correction but not the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold. Adding LC and LDTg volumes to the hierarchical logistic regression improved fit beyond disease duration, depressive symptoms, immediate verbal recall, and semantic fluency. These findings suggest that reduced MRI-derived volume of the left LDTg, and possibly of the left LC, is associated with early hallucination-related vulnerability in PD.

title: A DPP6-Targeted PET Tracer for Non-Invasive Imaging of Transplanted Human Islets.
abstract: Introduction Dipeptidyl peptidase-like protein 6 (DPP6) is a potential molecular imaging biomarker for pancreatic and transplanted islets of Langerhans. 4hD29 is a single-domain antibody with nanomolar affinity for DPP6. Here, we demonstrate the generation and validation of [ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-4hD29 for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging of human stem cell-derived islets (SC-islets) and human islets. Methods The binding of fluorescently labelled 4hD29 to human islets, human beta cell models and pancreatic tissues from various species over time was characterised. NOTA-4hD29 was radiolabelled with Gallium-68, and the resulting tracer [ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-4hD29 was evaluated for in vitro DPP6 binding as well as in vivo biodistribution. In vivo PET imaging was performed in immunodeficient mice transplanted with 400 to 800 SC-islets or human islets, and the uptake signal was compared to non-transplanted control mice. Results Fluorescently labelled 4hD29 demonstrated specific binding and internalisation in human islets. Fluorescence signal remained detectable for up to 2 h following incubation, indicating sustained intracellular retention. [ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-4hD29 bound to human islets with high specificity, and binding intensity correlated to islet purity. The binding of fluorescent and radiolabelled 4hD29 was negligible in extra-pancreatic tissues. In vivo PET imaging enabled reliable detection of grafts comprised of 400 to 800 SC-islets or human islets in immunodeficient mice. Conclusion [ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-4hD29 is a promising PET tracer for in vivo imaging of DPP6 in human islets. The tracer enabled non-invasive detection of transplanted human islet grafts in the 400-800 IEQ range and demonstrated favourable biodistribution and dosimetry profiles, supporting its further development for islet imaging applications.

title: The STEMI Mimic: Cocaine-Associated Pulmonary Embolism With ST-Segment Elevation.
abstract: Cocaine has been linked to both myocardial infarction (MI) and pulmonary embolism (PE), with the latter occasionally mimicking acute coronary syndrome. We report a 54-year-old man with polysubstance abuse who was found unresponsive and revived with naloxone. He developed chest pain with electrocardiogram showing ST-segment elevation in V2-V3 and elevated troponin, suggestive of anteroseptal ST-elevation MI (STEMI). Bedside echocardiography revealed right ventricular dilation and dysfunction without left ventricular abnormalities, prompting computed tomography angiography (CTA), which demonstrated large bilateral pulmonary emboli with right heart strain. He was anticoagulated and later discharged on a direct oral anticoagulant; coronary angiography revealed only mild nonobstructive disease. This case underscores the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing PE from STEMI in patients with cocaine use and highlights the utility of point-of-care echocardiography in avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures. Clinicians should consider PE in the differential diagnosis of chest pain with ST elevation.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Drainage via Thyroid Catheterization for Acute Suppurative Thyroiditis: A Case Report.
abstract: Background Acute suppurative thyroiditis (AST) is a rare but potentially life-threatening infection of the thyroid gland that requires prompt diagnosis and management. While antibiotic therapy remains the cornerstone of treatment, surgical intervention is often necessary in cases complicated by abscess formation. Minimally invasive approaches have emerged as alternative strategies. Case presentation A 49-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a rapidly enlarging painful neck mass, dysphagia, and radiating pain. title: Management of an Advanced Low-Lying Implantation Disorder With Cervico-Isthmic Features at 29 Weeks of Gestation Presenting With PPROM: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Introduction Cervico-isthmic pregnancy (CIP) is a rare form of low-lying implantation in which the gestational sac implants between the anatomical and histological internal os. It is associated with significant maternal morbidity due to abnormal placentation and a high risk of placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). Advanced cases beyond 20 weeks are exceedingly rare and pose major diagnostic and surgical challenges. Case presentation A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, with a history of prior cesarean section and Asherman syndrome, presented at 28 weeks and 4 days of gestation with preterm premature rupture of membranes. An ultrasound revealed a viable breech fetus located in the lower uterine segment and cervico-isthmic region. The presence of placental lacunae and bridging vessels suggested PAS. An MRI confirmed significant thinning of the lower uterine segment, nearly complete loss of myometrial tissue, and a preserved endocervical canal, consistent with CIP and PAS. Because of the high risk of hemorrhage, a cesarean section was performed using a posterior uterine incision, followed by immediate hysterectomy due to massive bleeding. Histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of placenta increta in the cervico-isthmic area. Both maternal recovery and neonatal outcomes were favorable. Discussion This case highlights the diagnostic difficulty of advanced low-lying implantation disorders with features favoring CIP. In late gestation, the anatomic boundaries among CIP, cervical pregnancy, and endogenic/Type I CSP may become difficult to define because the implantation site can expand beyond its original location. Careful evaluation of placental topography using ultrasound and MRI, supported by intraoperative anatomic findings and histopathologic correlation, can help characterize the implantation site and guide diagnostic interpretation. Nevertheless, even with multimodal assessment, overlap between CIP and endogenic/Type I CSP may persist, and definitive classification may remain challenging.

title: Absolute myocardial mass difference and ventriculo-arterial coupling in morphologically defined left ventricular non-compaction: A multiparametric cardiovascular magnetic resonance study.
abstract: BackgroundLeft ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) is increasingly recognized as a morphological phenotype rather than a distinct cardiomyopathy. Current cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) criteria rely predominantly on static morphologic thresholds and may not adequately reflect dynamic myocardial adaptation.PurposeTo investigate whether absolute myocardial mass difference (AD) represents a marker of structural-functional remodeling and to assess its relationship with hemodynamic and flow-related parameters in morphologically defined LVNC.Material and MethodsIn this retrospective study, 99 patients fulfilling Petersen and Grothoff CMR criteria for LVNC and 66 frequency-matched controls underwent multiparametric 1.5-T CMR. Volumetric indices, left atrial volume, cine-derived functional parameters, and aortic phase-contrast MRI flow timing indices, including time-to-peak velocity (TPV), ejection time (ET), and TPV/ET ratio, were analyzed. AD was defined as the indexed difference between end-diastolic myocardial mass and cycle-averaged myocardial mass. Between-group comparisons, effect size analysis, correlation testing, and ROC analysis were performed.ResultsAD was significantly higher in LVNC patients than in controls (3.71 ± 2.43 vs. 2.03 ± 1.49 g/m 2 ; P < 0.001) and demonstrated a large effect size (Cohen's d = 0.81). LVNC patients exhibited increased end-diastolic and end-systolic volume indices (both P < 0.001), preserved cardiac index, and altered systolic flow timing characteristics. AD correlated positively with left atrial volume ( r = 0.39; P < 0.001) and cardiac index ( r = 0.27; P = 0.007), whereas no significant association was observed with TPV/ET. ROC analysis demonstrated modest discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.71).ConclusionIn morphologically defined LVNC, AD is increased and associated with atrial remodeling and preserved hemodynamic adaptation. These findings suggest that AD may represent a marker of dynamic structural-functional remodeling rather than static trabecular excess. Incorporation of AD into multiparametric CMR assessment may improve phenotypic characterization and help distinguish compensated hypertrabecularization from clinically relevant myocardial disease.

title: A Silent Killer in an Unlikely Place: Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Breast.
abstract: Background: Primary necrotizing fasciitis (NF) of the breast is a rare, life-threatening soft tissue infection that is frequently misdiagnosed due to its non-specific early presentation and uncommon anatomical location. Objective: We report a case of primary NF of the breast to highlight the diagnostic challenges posed by atypical risk factors and the critical importance of timely surgical intervention and antibiotic cover. Methods: A 66-year-old female presented with breast pain, erythema, and systemic symptoms in the setting of hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) being treated with adalimumab and long-standing tobacco use. Clinical assessment, laboratory investigations, and computed tomography (CT) imaging were performed, followed by surgical exploration. Results: Initial concerns included abscess formation, cellulitis, or a HS flare. However, clinical instability and CT imaging demonstrated a gas-filled structure in the medial left breast with a developing gas-filled collection. Surgical exploration revealed extensive necrotising fasciitis involving the medial quadrant of the inner breast and underlying fascia, necessitating emergent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy. The patient required further debridement and wound management, followed by delayed reconstruction. Conclusion: This case illustrates how underlying risk factors, particularly immunosuppression, may predispose patients to atypical presentations of NF and reinforces the importance of early surgical and antibiotic intervention when clinical suspicion is high.

title: Eisenmenger Syndrome After Delayed Atrial Septal Defect Closure at High Altitude: A Case Report.
abstract: BACKGROUND Eisenmenger syndrome develops from untreated or late-repaired cardiac shunts, causing irreversible pulmonary-vascular remodeling and systemic symptoms. Although timely repair has nearly eradicated Eisenmenger syndrome in high-income regions, delayed diagnosis in middle-income countries, especially when combined with chronic high-altitude hypobaric hypoxia, such as at approximately 2800 m (9186 ft) in the Ecuadorian Andes, can accelerate pulmonary hypertension through hypoxic vasoconstriction and erythrocytosis. We report a case of Eisenmenger syndrome 2 decades after surgical atrial septal defect closure. CASE REPORT A 46-year-old woman living at high altitude presented with severe cyanosis and heart failure 22 years after atrial septal defect closure. She had marked hypoxemia and secondary erythrocytosis. Echocardiography showed suprasystemic pulmonary artery pressure, severe right-chamber dilation, and reduced right ventricular systolic function. Right-heart catheterization confirmed Eisenmenger physiology with severe pulmonary-vascular resistance and low cardiac index. Chest computed tomography showed marked pulmonary artery enlargement without thromboembolic disease. Multidisciplinary management included bosentan 125 mg twice daily, tadalafil 10 mg once daily, nocturnal oxygen, diuretics, and anticoagulation, resulting in symptomatic stabilization and discharge on day 4. Transplant evaluation was initiated. CONCLUSIONS Delayed atrial septal defect repair at high altitude can lead to irreversible Eisenmenger syndrome, for which current therapy is palliative. Early defect recognition and closure, congenital heart screening, and access to pulmonary vasodilators and transplant programs are imperative in resource-constrained mountainous regions.

title: Binary dermoscopic classification inadequately stratifies urgent and convenience excision decisions in community dermatology practice.
abstract: Dermoscopy is traditionally framed as a binary benign-malignant tool. Yet real-world practice uses multi-level triage: dermatologists allocate lesions to urgent excision, non-urgent excision, or surveillance based on dermoscopic atypia, contextual factors, and surveillance feasibility. Convenience excisions -low-suspicion lesions removed when monitoring is impractical - are a common, unacknowledged pattern. Dermoscopic literature reports only binary outcomes, ignoring this process. To evaluate whether clinical urgency classification captures melanoma risk beyond isolated dermoscopic assessment in community practice with limited surveillance capacity. We retrospectively analysed 371 consecutively excised melanocytic lesions. Two blinded dermatologists independently assigned four-level gestalt atypia scores. Referring dermatologists prospectively classified excisions as urgent or non-urgent, integrating morphological concern with surveillance constraints. Histopathology identified melanoma prevalence and number needed to excise (NNE). Multivariable regression evaluated predictors of melanoma. Melanoma prevalence was 23.2% (86 melanomas: 41 in situ, 45 invasive; NNE=4.3). Inter-rater agreement for morphology-only assessment was poor (κ=0.16), with weak histopathological correlation (ρ=0.23-0.29). Most excisions (75%) were non-urgent, predominantly convenience excisions, yet captured 44 of 86 melanomas (51%). For invasive melanoma alone, NNE rose to 8.2, still favourable versus the 1:10 benchmark. Age predicted melanoma-in situ diagnoses, but age-stratified analysis showed no disproportionate overdiagnosis. Clinical urgency -which integrates morphological concern with contextual factors and shares information with dermoscopic assessment- predicted melanoma (OR=3.05, p=0.002) beyond gestalt scores, age, and phenotypic complexity. Binary dermoscopic frameworks inadequately reflect real-world multi-factorial triage. Effective melanoma detection depends on integrating morphology with patient-specific risk and system-level factors beyond dermoscopy alone.

title: Management of Complications of a Fulminant Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) Associated with Myocarditis and Left Ventricular Thrombus Under VA-ECMO: A Case Report of a Novel Thrombectomy Technique with Pulsed Irrigation and Review of Left and Right Ventricular Unloading Techniques
abstract: Fulminant Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) associated with myocarditis is rare but may result in severe myocardial dysfunction requiring veno-arterial extracorporeal mem-brane oxygenation (VA-ECMO), which itself increases the risk of left ventricular (LV) distension and thrombus formation. We report the case of a 50-year-old woman who developed refractory cardiogenic shock following out-of-hospital ventricular fibrilla-tion cardiac arrest and required peripheral VA-ECMO. VZV DNA was detected in the blood, while coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries, support-ing a diagnosis of fulminant VZV-associated myocarditis. Despite anticoagulation and multimodal LV unloading with an intra-aortic balloon pump and Rashkind atrial sep-tostomy, persistent LV distension and absence of aortic valve opening were followed by formation of a large and organized LV thrombus. After neurological assessment confirmed preserved responsiveness, surgical thrombectomy was undertaken. Thrombus removal was performed through the aortic valve and mitral valve, followed by pulsed irrigation of the LV cavity and surgical apical venting connected to the ECMO venous circuit. Histopathology demonstrated lymphocytic myocarditis of probable viral origin. The patient subsequently developed multiorgan failure and died on postoperative day six. This case highlights the challenges of thrombus formation during VA-ECMO and the importance of early, individualized ventricular unloading. We additionally review available left ventricular unloading strategies and right ven-tricular unloading techniques in patients requiring VA-ECMO, emphasizing their re-spective indications and technical considerations.

title: MedBackdoorGuard: Detecting and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Deep Learning Models for MRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment Diagnosis
abstract: Deep learning classifiers trained on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are increasingly proposed for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), yet the pipelines that produce these models depend on shared datasets, pre-trained weights, and federated updates that an adversary can poison. A backdoored diagnostic model behaves correctly on ordinary scans but collapses to an attacker-chosen label whenever a hidden trigger is present, which turns a prognostic instrument for cognitive aging into a silent source of misdiagnosis. This article proposes MedBackdoorGuard, a defense framework that detects and mitigates backdoor attacks in MRI-based AD and MCI classifiers without prior knowledge of the trigger. The framework couples spectral latent screening of training data with latent trigger isolation in activation space, then immunizes the model through trigger-sensitive neuron pruning and fine-tuning under an anatomical attention consistency constraint that anchors the decision on medial temporal structures. A runtime inference guard adds superimposition entropy and anatomically informed reconstruction to purify suspicious scans at deployment. Across ADNI, OASIS-1, and a public four-class dementia MRI benchmark under patch, blended, warping, and frequency triggers, MedBackdoorGuard reduces the mean attack success rate from 97.4% to 3.0% while holding clean accuracy within 0.6 percentage points of the undefended model, reaches a poisoned-sample detection AUROC of 97.4%, and identifies 59 of 60 backdoored models. Compared with the strongest defense baseline, attack success rate falls by 15.1 percentage points and clean accuracy rises by 1.7 percentage points. The framework restores MCI recall on triggered scans from 3.9% to 88.3%, which is the outcome that matters for early detection in cognitive aging.

Across ADNI, OASIS-1, and a public four-class dementia MRI benchmark under patch, blended, warping, and frequency triggers, MedBackdoorGuard reduces the mean attack success rate from 97.4% to 3.0% while holding clean accuracy within 0.6 percentage points of the undefended model, reaches a poisoned-sample detection AUROC of 97.4%, and identifies 59 of 60 backdoored models. Compared with the strongest defense baseline, attack success rate falls by 15.1 percentage points and clean accuracy rises by 1.7 percentage points. The framework restores MCI recall on triggered scans from 3.9% to 88.3%, which is the outcome that matters for early detection in cognitive aging.

title: Pleomorphic Adenoma of the Upper Lip: A Case Report with Histopathological and Clinical Correlation
abstract: Abstract Background Pleomorphic adenoma (PA), often called benign mixed tumour is the most common salivary gland neoplasm. Majority of the tumours occur in major salivary glands from while only 10% occurs in minor salivary glands. Cases of PA in the oral cavity have been mainly reported in palate and respectively in the upper lip. Case presentation In this case report, we describe a case of pleomorphic adenoma with a rare clinical feature. A 49-year-old female reported to the dental hospital with a complain of slowly developing reddish-yellow coloured painless swelling in the left upper labial vestibule since 5 years. Temporary pain and temperature sensitivity have also been reported. Radiographically, there is no evidence of any radiolucency. Hence, Lipoma, mucocele, minor salivary gland tumour was considered as the differential diagnosis as these lesions are also reported in the upper lip, and they can show these clinical features. An excisional biopsy was taken. It shows a biphasic proliferation of epithelial cells and myoepithelial cells in cords and well-defined aggregates in a mixed myxoid/chondroid stroma. It shows a well-circumscribed lesion features typical for PA of the upper lip. The post-operative period was uneventful, and on 3-month follow-up, no recurrence was noted. Conclusions Pleomorphic adenoma of the upper lip is an uncommon benign neoplasm that should be included in the differential diagnosis of persistent mucosal swellings. This case highlights the importance of histopathological confirmation to ensure optimal patient outcomes.

title: Acute coma with severe infection events: a population-based retrospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Previous studies shown that acute coma is a very common public health issuer in global. However, the prevalence and high risk of death in acute coma with severe infection events(SIE) remains understudied. We aimed to investigate whether acute coma with high risk of death is related to SIE so that to improve its outcome. Metholds A retrospective study of adult acute coma patients with or without SIE is conducted from a teaching hospital sites in China. The patients who were underwent a systemic (I.e, brain lungs and abdomen) CT screening before ICU and confirmed wiith or without SIE is included in this study. The primary outcome is the prevalence and high risk of death from acute coma with SIE. Logistic or Cox proportional Hazard models with cubic sening. Results: From January 1, 2018, to Jamuary 1, 2023. A total of 1180 patients with acute coma were admitted to the ICU. We found that 839(70.4%) patients had SIE and 349(29.6%) did not. Of these, 64.3% were male, with a mean age of 66.8 years (SD, 16.3). Initial median Glasgow Coma Scales (GCS) score was 6.0 (IQR 3 to 8). In the ICU stay, 69.3% underwent invasive mechanical ventilation due to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Community- acquired pneumonia (82.1%, 969/1180) was the most common infection. There was significant differences in the potential risk factors for coma with SIE or without SIE. Adjusted odds ratio [aOR] achieved 6.9 (95% confidence intervals[CI] 4.30-7.48) for acute coma with SIE, 5.3(4,25-5.82) for extended cytokine storm duration, 3.5 (95% CI, 2.82- 5.17) for elevated SOFA scores, and 3.0(95%CI,2.18 - 4.83 ) for elevated cytokine levels. The aOR of coma with SIE was the highest as compared with the other risk factors. At the 28 days follow-up, survival rate was significantly lower among with SIE than without SIE ( HR for death, 3.1; p,0.001) and most died in the ICU. Conclusions: Highly prevalent acute coma with high risk of death is associated with SIE, supporting that acute coma should used an early systemic CT screening to identify SIE, and facilitate early treatment to improve outcomes.

title: Erdheim–Chester disease with cardiac involvement confirmed by biopsy: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background： Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD) is a rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis which manifests as uncontrolled proliferation and infiltration across multiple systems. Cardiovascular involvement is quite common, which is associated with poor prognosis. However, patients often lack prominent cardiovascular symptoms, making diagnosis difficult. Most published cardiac ECD diagnoses rely solely on imaging findings; cases with histopathological confirmation via cardiac tissue biopsy remain extremely scarce. Case presentation: This report describes a 44-year-old woman with 6-month recurrent fevers, multiple prior admissions. Positron Emission Tomography–Computed Tomography (PET-CT) showed a progressive increase in fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in the soft tissue surrounding the right atrium; echocardiography detected a circumferential heterogeneous mass on the right heart wall plus pericardial effusion. Open cardiac biopsy confirmed non-Langerhans histiocytic proliferation. NGS found MAP2K1 mutation without BRAF V600E alteration, and bone scan showed long bone uptake, verifying ECD. The patient is currently receiving interferon-α (IFN-α) therapy. Conclusions: This is a case of cardiac ECD that was pathologically diagnosed through an open cardiac biopsy. Through the summary of this case and a concise review of cases of ECD with cardiac involvement, we can enhance the understanding of the potential clinical, imaging, and histopathological manifestations of this rare disease, thereby reducing the rates of misdiagnosis and missed diagnosis.

title: Cascade Deep Learning (nnU-Net + ResNet-18) for Meniscus Segmentation and Three-Grade Injury Classification on Knee MRI: A Single-Centre Study with Reader Assistance Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Background Accurate detection and grading of meniscal injury guide treatment, but MRI interpretation is time-consuming and subject to interobserver variability. We developed and evaluated a cascade deep-learning framework that segments the menisci and grades their status (healthy, degenerative, grade-III tear) on knee MRI, and assessed its value as a reader-assistance tool. Methods In this single-centre retrospective study, 562 patients (608 knees; 1,216 coronal and sagittal sequences) scanned on a 1.5-T system between 2018 and 2022 were included. A 3D nnU-Net segmented the medial and lateral menisci. Subsequently, the segmented regions of interest were classified by a 2D ResNet-18 into three grades, and coronal and sagittal predictions were fused by a most-severe-class rule.The dataset was partitioned at the patient level into an 80% training set and a 20% held-out test set. Model performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), accuracy, F1 score, and the area under the ROC curve (AUC). In a multi-reader study, two junior readers diagnosed 100 cases, first unaided and subsequently, following a two-week washout period, with AI assistance (probabilities and Grad-CAM maps). Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for grade-III tears, reading time, and inter-reader agreement were compared using the McNemar test and Cohen’s κ. Results The nnU-Net achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.84 for intact menisci, but only 0.32–0.40 for injured menisci. For binary detection (torn vs. non-torn), the fusion model reached an accuracy of 73.77% (F1-score: 72.88%), with the coronal plane outperforming the sagittal plane (F1-score: 76.29% vs. 68.83%; AUC: 0.79 vs. 0.71); the three-grade accuracy was 68.01%. With AI assistance, the accuracy of junior readers increased from 64.0% to 78.0% (McNemar χ² = 7.68, P < 0.01), sensitivity for grade-III tears improved from 60.0% to 80.0%, reading time decreased by 38% (from 44.7 ± 11.2 to 27.9 ± 7.4 s/case), and interobserver agreement improved from κ = 0.52 to 0.68. Conclusion The cascade nnU-Net + ResNet-18 framework performed meniscus segmentation and injury grading with moderate standalone accuracy but demonstrated a clear assistive benefit, improving the sensitivity and efficiency of junior readers. This framework may serve as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for expert interpretation.

title: Giant Pericardial Cyst in the Right Cardiophrenic Angle Mimicking a Hydatid Cyst: A Case Report of a Diagnostic Challenge in an Endemic Region
abstract: Abstract Rationale : Pericardial cysts are rare benign mediastinal lesions, representing approximately 10–20% of all mediastinal masses, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 100,000 persons [1,2]. While most are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, giant cysts may present with non-specific symptoms mimicking other thoracic pathologies. The majority of pericardial cysts are located in the right cardiophrenic angle (77%) [1,3]. Patient concerns : We report the case of a 57-year-old Syrian male smoker who presented with grade I exertional dyspnea without cough or constitutional symptoms. A chest radiograph performed during routine evaluation revealed a homogeneous density in the right lower lung field. Diagnoses : Chest imaging, including computed tomography (CT), revealed a giant pericardial cyst measuring up to 14.75 cm in greatest dimension, located in the right anterior cardiophrenic angle. The diagnosis was subsequently confirmed by histopathological examination following complete surgical excision. Interventions : The patient underwent complete surgical excision of the pericardial cyst via right posterolateral thoracotomy through the fifth intercostal space, with intraoperative aspiration of clear fluid contents to facilitate safe removal. Outcomes : The patient's symptoms resolved completely following surgical intervention. Chest tube drainage was 500 mL on day 1 and decreased to 80 mL on day 2, with complete lung expansion confirmed radiographically. The chest tube was removed on postoperative day 2, and the patient was discharged home on postoperative day 3 in stable condition. Follow-up was scheduled at 2 weeks and 2 months postoperatively. Lessons : This case emphasizes the importance of including pericardial cysts in the differential diagnosis of patients with non-specific thoracic symptoms, particularly in regions where echinococcosis is endemic. Elevated anti-echinococcal antibodies (Echinococcus Ab 1/320 positive) initially suggested a hydatid cyst, which was misleading and posed a diagnostic challenge. While video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is the preferred minimally invasive approach, open thoracotomy remains a safe and effective option for giant cysts with extensive adhesions or challenging anatomical locations [1].

title: Clinical and CT radiomics-based differentiation between invasive pulmonary fungal infections and secondary pulmonary tuberculosis
abstract: Abstract Background Worldwide diagnoses of invasive pulmonary fungal infection (IPFI) have increased steadily in recent years. Because the clinical manifestations and computed tomography (CT) findings of IPFI frequently resemble those of secondary pulmonary tuberculosis, distinguishing between these two conditions remains challenging and often leads to delayed or incorrect diagnosis. This study was devised with the goal of creating and validating a model for IPFI prediction utilizing clinical and CT radiomics characteristics for distinguishing between IPFI and secondary tuberculosis. Methods In this retrospective multicenter study, 153 patients with IPFI and 130 patients with secondary tuberculosis were recruited from two tertiary medical centers between January 1, 2020, and May 31, 2024. Individuals were randomly allocated to training and validation cohorts (7:3). Factors found to be independently predictive of IPFI by multivariable logistic regression were used to establish a clinical model. Radiomics features were selected through variance thresholding, univariate feature selection, and LASSO logistic regression to generate a radiomics score (Rad-score). A combined model including both clinical and radiomics predictors was subsequently developed and compared with the diagnostic performance of junior and senior radiologists. Model discrimination was evaluated via ROC curves, while utility was examined using decision curve analysis. Results Multivariable logistic regression identified long-term broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, hemoglobin concentration, and neutrophil count as independent clinical predictors of IPFI. The Rad-score was derived from 18 radiomics characteristics with non-zero coefficients after selection using LASSO regression. The integrated clinical-radiomics model showed excellent discrimination, with AUCs of 0.880 (95% CI, 0.834–0.926) in the training set and 0.844 (95% CI, 0.761–0.926) in the validation set. This model also outperformed both senior and junior radiologists in the validation cohort when distinguishing IPFI from secondary tuberculosis Conclusion A model for IPFI prediction based on clinical and CT-based radiomics characteristics demonstrated strong diagnostic performance for differentiating IPFI from secondary tuberculosis. This approach provides an objective, quantitative tool to facilitate the early identification of IPFI and support clinical decision-making.

title: Development and External Validation of a Risk Score for Post-Appendectomy Intra-Abdominal Infection
abstract: Abstract Background. Intra-abdominal infection (IAI) following appendectomy is a serious complication associated with prolonged hospitalization, repeated interventions, and increased morbidity. No universally accepted risk-stratification tool exists to guide individualized perioperative management or antimicrobial stewardship decisions after appendectomy. Objective. To identify independent preoperative and intraoperative predictors of post-appendectomy IAI and to develop a simple, clinically usable risk-stratification score to support perioperative decision-making and tailored antibiotic strategies. Methods. A retrospective analytical cohort study conducted at the General Surgery Department, CTGB, Ben Arous, Tunisia, over 24 months (January 2023–December 2023). All patients aged ≥ 14 years operated on for confirmed acute appendicitis were included. IAI was defined as a symptomatic intra-abdominal collection confirmed by imaging and/or drainage within 30 postoperative days. Univariate analysis and parsimonious multivariate logistic regression were performed. A bedside risk score (IAI-Risk Score) was derived from independent predictors and internally validated by stratification. Results. Of 400 patients (median age 32 years; 55% male), IAI occurred in 12 cases (3.0%). Four independent predictors were identified by parsimonious multivariate analysis: appendiceal peritonitis (aOR 5.12; 95% CI 3.54–9.42; p = 0.001), elevated CRP > 80.5 mg/L (aOR 4.22; 95% CI 1.60–14.87; p = 0.001), gangrenous appendicitis (aOR 2.22; 95% CI 1.52–4.28; p = 0.028), and appendicolith on CT (aOR 1.82; 95% CI 1.38–8.80; p = 0.001). CRP demonstrated excellent discriminative performance (AUC 0.892; 95% CI 0.827–0.958). The derived IAI-Risk Score stratified patients into low- (0%), intermediate- (5.4%), and high-risk (40.0%) groups. External validation in an independent cohort of 200 patients confirmed acceptable discriminative performance of the IAI-Risk Score (AUC 0.801; 95% CI [0.701–0.901]), supporting its generalizability beyond the derivation center. Conclusion. A parsimonious perioperative risk model combining inflammatory, radiological, and intraoperative parameters allows reliable stratification of post-appendectomy IAI risk. CRP > 80.5 mg/L, appendicolith, gangrenous appendicitis, and appendiceal peritonitis should trigger intensified postoperative surveillance and risk-adapted antibiotic strategies, supporting contemporary antimicrobial stewardship principles. External validation confirmed adequate generalizability of the score, supporting its integration into risk-adapted perioperative antibiotic and surveillance protocols after appendectomy.

title: Fragmented ownership and multilevel barriers to breast MRI screening among high-risk women: A qualitative study informing development of clinical decision support
abstract: Abstract Background: Women at high risk for breast cancer include those with pathogenic variants in hereditary breast cancer predisposition genes, high-risk benign breast lesions, or a lifetime risk over 20% based on validated models. Supplemental breast MRI screening improves early detection and reduces interval cancers in high-risk women. Despite recommendations from professional organizations for breast MRI screening among high-risk women, uptake remains low. To better understand breast MRI utilization, we conducted a qualitative study exploring healthcare provider and patient perspectives to inform development of a screening module within our patient-facing web-based decision aid, RealRisks . Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 women at high risk for breast cancer and 17 healthcare providers at an urban academic medical center in New York City. All interviews were transcribed verbatim and coded using Dedoose software. Transcripts were analyzed thematically to identify patterns in clinician communication strategies, MRI screening practices, as well as barriers and facilitators shaping implementation. Results: All enrolled providers were female, including six primary care providers (PCPs), five gynecologists, four breast radiologists, and two cancer genetic counselors. Among enrolled patients, mean age was 51.8 years (SD, 14.8) and 40% were Hispanic, 40% non-Hispanic White, 10% non-Hispanic Black, and 10% other. More than half of providers (59%) had ordered a breast MRI for high-risk patients, and 55% of patients had previously undergone MRI screening. The three themes that emerged included: 1) responsibility in initiating MRI screening was fragmented across specialties; 2) patients and providers encountered barriers at every step of the screening process, including knowledge gaps and uncertainty about insurance coverage; 3) both groups identified a need for clearer, consolidated guidelines and accessible resources to support informed decision-making. Conclusion: Our findings highlight the need to address structural and communication barriers to improve MRI screening uptake among high-risk women and their providers . Integrating electronic medical record (EMR)-based risk assessment and patient educational materials into clinical workflows may support informed, shared decision-making. Future work will involve design and usability testing of the RealRisks screening module, which will be available in English and Spanish and tailored to patients with varying health literacy and educational backgrounds.

Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 women at high risk for breast cancer and 17 healthcare providers at an urban academic medical center in New York City. All interviews were transcribed verbatim and coded using Dedoose software. Transcripts were analyzed thematically to identify patterns in clinician communication strategies, MRI screening practices, as well as barriers and facilitators shaping implementation. Results: All enrolled providers were female, including six primary care providers (PCPs), five gynecologists, four breast radiologists, and two cancer genetic counselors. Among enrolled patients, mean age was 51.8 years (SD, 14.8) and 40% were Hispanic, 40% non-Hispanic White, 10% non-Hispanic Black, and 10% other. More than half of providers (59%) had ordered a breast MRI for high-risk patients, and 55% of patients had previously undergone MRI screening. The three themes that emerged included: 1) responsibility in initiating MRI screening was fragmented across specialties; 2) patients and providers encountered barriers at every step of the screening process, including knowledge gaps and uncertainty about insurance coverage; 3) both groups identified a need for clearer, consolidated guidelines and accessible resources to support informed decision-making. Conclusion: Our findings highlight the need to address structural and communication barriers to improve MRI screening uptake among high-risk women and their providers . Integrating electronic medical record (EMR)-based risk assessment and patient educational materials into clinical workflows may support informed, shared decision-making. Future work will involve design and usability testing of the RealRisks screening module, which will be available in English and Spanish and tailored to patients with varying health literacy and educational backgrounds.

title: Cross-validated radiomic SuStaIn identifies prognostically and transcriptomically distinct event-ordering phenotypes in diffuse glioma
abstract: Abstract Background Current histomolecular classifications do not fully explain outcome heterogeneity within diffuse glioma, while most radiomic approaches use static prediction or clustering. We evaluated whether Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) could identify MRI-derived event-ordering phenotypes with prognostic and biological relevance. Methods This retrospective analysis included 246 patients with glioblastoma or lower-grade glioma from the public RadGLO resource. SuStaIn models with one to three subtypes were fitted to eight predefined contrast-enhanced T1-weighted radiomic features and compared by five-fold cross-validation. Survival associations were evaluated using subtype assignments, posterior probabilities, and grade and IDH subgroup analyses. Matched RNA sequencing from 194 patients was analyzed using limma-voom and gene-set enrichment analysis. Results A two-subtype model provided the lowest cross-validation information criterion. S1 showed early shape-irregularity and multiscale kurtosis abnormalities, whereas S2 showed early compactness and wavelet intensity/texture abnormalities. S2 was associated with higher mortality after adjustment for age and grade (hazard ratio 1.77, 95% confidence interval 1.23–2.54; p = 0.002). Each 0.10 increase in S2 probability was associated with 9.2% higher mortality risk (p = 0.005) and remained significant after additional IDH adjustment (p = 0.017). Subgroup estimates were directionally consistent, with no interaction by grade or IDH status. Transcriptomic analyses linked S2 to translation, ribosome biogenesis, DNA replication, and chromosome segregation, and S1 to neuronal and synaptic programs. Conclusions Radiomic SuStaIn identified two event-ordering phenotypes that provided prognostic information beyond established clinical and molecular classifications and showed distinct transcriptomic correlates. Independent validation with harmonized and longitudinal imaging is required.

title: Ultrasound Viscoelastic Parameters of Distal Breast Tissue in Molecular Subtyping and Prognosis of Luminal Breast Cancer: A Preliminary Imaging-Transcriptomic Study
abstract: Abstract Purpose To investigate the predictive value of ultrasound viscoelastic parameters of distal breast tissue for molecular subtyping (Luminal A vs. Luminal B) and prognosis of breast cancer, and to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms through transcriptomic analysis. Methods A total of 77 patients with pathologically confirmed Luminal-type breast cancer (32 Luminal A, 45 Luminal B) were prospectively enrolled from January 2023 to April 2024. All patients underwent ultrasound viscoelastic imaging to measure elasticity and viscosity parameters in the tumor (T), peritumoral (P), and distal breast tissue (N) regions. Whole-transcriptome sequencing was performed on T, P, and N tissue samples from three Luminal B patients. ROC curves were used to evaluate diagnostic performance, and Spearman correlation and logistic regression were applied to assess associations with prognosis. Results Viscoelastic parameters of distal breast tissue differed significantly between Luminal A and Luminal B subtypes (all P < 0.05), while T and P region parameters showed no differences. N-VMean achieved an AUC of 0.724 for predicting Luminal B subtype (specificity 91.1%) and an AUC of 0.733 for predicting poor prognosis. Transcriptomic analysis identified 10 key genes (including COL11A1 and WASF3) differentially expressed between T and P regions, enriched in ECM-receptor interaction, focal adhesion, and cell junction pathways. Conclusion Viscoelastic parameters of distal breast tissue, particularly viscosity, can effectively distinguish Luminal A from Luminal B subtypes and show promising prognostic value. The underlying mechanisms may involve ECM remodeling and cytoskeletal regulation, positioning distal tissue as a potential novel imaging biomarker for non-invasive prognostic assessment in breast cancer.

title: Impact of Three-Dimensional Computed Tomography Reconstruction on Clinical Decision-Making in Revisional Bariatric Surgery
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Revisional bariatric surgery is increasingly common because of weight regain, insufficient weight loss, and postoperative anatomical complications, but conventional imaging often fails to provide comprehensive anatomical characterization. Three-dimensional (3D) computed tomography (CT)-based modeling may improve anatomical evaluation and surgical planning, but its impact on clinical decision-making remains insufficiently explored. Methods This retrospective, cross-sectional study included 40 consecutive patients referred for revisional bariatric evaluation between January 2021 and December 2024 at a tertiary referral center. All patients underwent standardized CT acquisition, 3D reconstruction, and gastric volumetric analysis, and were classified into a surgical group (n = 28) or a conservative management group (n = 12) after multidisciplinary assessment. The primary outcome was change in therapeutic management after 3D evaluation; secondary outcomes included weight-loss results, detection of anatomical abnormalities, gastric volumetry, and interobserver reproducibility. Results 3D modeling changed therapeutic decision-making in 42.5% of cases. Surgical plans were cancelled in 20.0% of patients, and 22.5% were reclassified for revisional surgery after 3D anatomical assessment. Anatomical abnormalities were identified in 75.0% of patients, including sleeve dilation (35.0%), intrathoracic gastric migration (15.0%), internal hernias (12.0%), and complex fistulas (8.0%). Gastric volumetry correlated strongly with weight-loss outcomes (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). Patients undergoing revisional surgery achieved significantly greater total weight loss than those managed conservatively (65.0% vs. 12.0%). Interobserver agreement for volumetric measurements was excellent (ICC = 0.96). Conclusion CT-based 3D modeling significantly influenced therapeutic decision-making in revisional bariatric surgery by improving anatomical characterization, identifying clinically relevant abnormalities, and supporting patient selection. These findings support 3D reconstruction as an adjunct in the multidisciplinary evaluation of revisional bariatric patients and warrant validation in prospective multicenter studies.

title: Development and Validation of a Feature-Prompted Deep Learning System for Diagnosing Chronic Atrophic Gastritis Under White-Light Endoscopy
abstract: Abstract Background Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is a precancerous condition whose endoscopic detection under white-light endoscopy (WLE) is limited by low sensitivity and high inter-observer variability. We aimed to develop and validate an end-to-end artificial intelligence (AI) system for CAG diagnosis during WLE and compare it with endoscopists of different experience levels. Methods We conducted a single-center retrospective study in which an AI system with three sequential deep learning modules (image quality assessment, anatomical site classification, and atrophy detection) was trained and validated on data from 943 patients. The atrophy detection module used a feature-prompted strategy: segmentation masks were applied to focus the classifier on suspected atrophic regions. The best model was compared with six endoscopists (four intermediate, two senior) on an independent test set, with histopathology as the reference standard. Results The feature-prompted model (DCNN3a-1) reached a sensitivity of 92.4%, specificity of 89.2%, and accuracy of 90.9%. Its accuracy was not significantly different from that of senior endoscopists (90.9% vs. 90.3%, p = 0.738) but was higher than that of intermediate endoscopists (85.6%, p < 0.001) and the overall endoscopist group (87.2%, p < 0.05). Conclusions The AI system achieves expert-level CAG diagnostic performance under WLE. The feature-prompted approach improves accuracy over whole-image classification and may help standardize CAG diagnosis in routine clinical practice.

title: Spatial artificial intelligence in gastric endoscopy for premalignant lesions and early gastric cancer: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence in gastric endoscopy increasingly produces spatial outputs to localize abnormal mucosa and define lesion extent, yet their clinical validity is uncertain. We conducted a task-specific systematic review nested within a prospectively registered parent review and identified 39 study families evaluating localization, segmentation, boundary identification, or margin delineation in gastric premalignant lesions and early gastric cancer. Most studies assessed segmentation on stored images. Histopathology often confirmed diagnosis, but spatial references were usually expert-defined endoscopic masks rather than pathology-registered boundaries. Only three studies reported patient-disjoint internal testing, six external validation, six a prospective component, and two live spatial evaluations; one study showed procedure-altering biopsy guidance. Dice, IoU, boundary, and margin measures were heterogeneous and were not pooled. Spatial AI has moved toward clinically relevant mapping and margin assessment, but stronger reference standards and validation during endoscopy are needed before these outputs can support procedural decisions.

title: Ultrasound-based deep learning-derived radiomics for preoperative prediction of sentinel lymph node metastasis in invasive breast cancer: a two-center retrospective study
abstract: Abstract Background Preoperative assessment of sentinel lymph node (SLN) metastasis may support individualized axillary management in patients with invasive breast cancer (IBC). We developed and externally validated a deep learning-derived ultrasound radiomics model for predicting SLN metastasis. Methods This retrospective two-center study included 246 patients with pathologically confirmed IBC. Center A provided 194 patients (93 with SLN metastasis), who were divided into training (n = 155) and internal test (n = 39) cohorts; 52 patients from Center B (20 with SLN metastasis) constituted an external validation cohort. Deep features were extracted from preoperative ultrasound images using a ResNet50 architecture. Feature selection was performed in the training cohort, and a gradient boosting decision tree classifier was developed. Discrimination was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis; decision curve analysis was performed as an exploratory assessment of net benefit. Results Twenty-two deep learning-derived features were retained for model development. The model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.734 (95% CI, 0.655–0.813) in the training cohort, 0.761 (95% CI, 0.601–0.920) in the internal test cohort, and 0.742 (95% CI, 0.598–0.886) in the external validation cohort. In the external cohort, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were 0.769, 0.650, 0.844, 0.722, and 0.794, respectively. Decision curves are reported as exploratory analyses and do not establish clinical utility. Conclusion A deep learning-derived ultrasound radiomics model showed moderate and relatively consistent discrimination for SLN metastasis across the development and external validation cohorts. These findings support further evaluation of the model as an adjunctive preoperative risk-stratification tool; prospective validation in larger and more diverse populations is required before clinical implementation.

title: Age at onset of hip osteoarthritis and joint survival in developmental dysplasia of the hip: a 20-year longitudinal study stratified by lateral center-edge angle
abstract: Abstract Background Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is a major cause of hip osteoarthritis (OA). However, few studies have evaluated OA onset age and joint preservation in relation to DDH severity. Here, we stratified DDH cases by lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) and analyzed age at radiographic OA onset and 20-year joint survival rates according to LCEA magnitude. Methods DDH cases were classified into six groups by LCEA: A, ≤ 5°; B, > 5° to ≤ 10°; C, > 10° to ≤ 15°; D, > 15° to ≤ 20°; E, > 20° to ≤ 25°; and F, > 25°. Age at OA onset was compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test. The endpoint was radiographic OA onset, and joint survival rates were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Results In total, 151 hips were followed for a mean of 24.8 years. The distribution was 15, 17, 48, 35, 25, and 11 hips in groups A to F, respectively. Age at OA onset was in the 50s to 60s in all groups, with no significant differences (p = 0.577). The 20-year joint survival rates were 40.0%, 77.8%, 71.6%, 81.4%, 79.2%, and 90.9%, respectively, with no significant difference (p = 0.138). Conclusions Radiographic OA onset in DDH occurred in the 50s to 60s regardless of LCEA magnitude. Although survival was lowest in group A and highest in group F, the overall comparison was not statistically significant. Prognosis is difficult to predict using LCEA alone, and further investigation incorporating other morphological parameters and patient background is warranted. Trial registration Not applicable.

title: Endometriosis/Adenomyosis and Congenital Uterine Malformations: Correlation of ESHRE/ESGE classes to #ENZIAN compartments
abstract: Abstract Purpose Identify the association between endometriosis/adenomyosis and Congenital Uterine Malformations (CUMs), determine the malformation most commonly associated and detect the #Enzian compartment most frequently involved. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 304 patients with CUMs diagnosed by three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound (3D-TVS) according to the ESHRE/ESGE classification, referred to our Gynecological Ultrasound Unit between January 2022 and December 2025. Concurrent endometriosis/adenomyosis was assessed by 2D/3D-TVS, and lesion distribution was analyzed according to the #Enzian classification. Results Among the 304 patients, 44 (14.5%) had dysmorphic uterus (ESHRE U1), 193 (63.5%) septate uterus (U2), 30 (9.8%) bicorporeal uterus (U3), 35 (11.5%) hemi-uterus (U4), and 2 (0.6%) aplastic uterus (U5). Overall, 116 patients (38.2%) showed at least one ultrasound sign of endometriosis/adenomyosis: 22/44 (50%) U1, 80/193 (41.5%) U2, 5/30 (16.7%) U3, 9/35 (25.7%) U4, and none with U5. U3 showed the lowest association with endometriosis/adenomyosis (OR 0.29). Multivariate logistic regression identified significant associations for U1 (OR 5.0) and U2 (OR 3.5). Analysis of the #Enzian compartments showed that U1 was associated with the FA compartment (OR 8.00), whereas U2 was associated with DIE compartment (A + B+C + FB; OR 5.16). No significant association was found for U3, U4, or U5. Conclusion CUMs are associated with endometriosis/adenomyosis and may influence lesion distribution. U2 is mainly associated with DIE, whereas U1 is primarily associated with the FA compartment. These findings support the integration of advanced 3D-TVS and the #Enzian classification in the assessment of patients with CUMs. Preoperative identification of anomaly-specific endometriotic patterns may improve diagnostic accuracy and guide minimally invasive surgical planning.

title: Giant Fibroepithelial Stromal Polyp of the Vulva Mimicking a Malignant Neoplasm: A Rare Case Report
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Fibroepithelial polyps (FEPs) of the vulva are uncommon benign mesenchymal lesions that typically measure less than 5 cm. Giant pedunculated FEPs arising from the labia majora are exceptionally rare and can clinically mimic malignant neoplasms. Case Presentation: We report a 29-year-old nulliparous, unmarried woman who presented with a rapidly enlarging, ulcerated, pedunculated vulvar mass arising from the right labia majora. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a pedunculated cutaneous and subcutaneous soft-tissue mass measuring 9.4 × 6.4 × 4.6 cm, with heterogeneous nodular enhancement suggestive of a vascularized tumor. The mass was completely excised at its pedicle base, with intraoperative ligation of two bleeding vessels at the stalk. Histopathology revealed a fibrovascular stromal core covered by stratified squamous epithelium, consistent with a fibroepithelial polyp, with foci of hemorrhagic infarction attributed to torsion of the stalk; no atypia or malignant features were identified. At one-month postoperative follow-up, the surgical site had healed normally. Conclusions: Giant vulvar FEPs are rare benign tumors that can mimic malignancy because of their unusual size, ulceration, and discharge, particularly with rapid growth. Complete surgical excision with secure control of the pedicle is curative, and histopathological confirmation is essential to exclude sarcomas and other soft-tissue neoplasms. This entity should be kept in the differential diagnosis of large vulvar masses to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary aggressive intervention. Short-term clinical follow-up is advisable to confirm healing and detect rare complications such as torsion-related infarction.

title: Cross-center sex estimation from patellar CT: multi-feature transformer fusion of morphometry, radiomics, and deep features
abstract: Abstract Patellar computed tomography (CT) images contain sex-dimorphic information; however, single-feature approaches may not fully exploit complementary information. We developed a multi-feature Transformer fusion framework integrating morphometry, radiomics, and deep learning features for sex estimation. We retrospectively included 836 knee CT scans from two centers: an internal dataset ( n = 697, slice thickness 1.5 mm) for model development and internal testing, and an external dataset ( n = 139, slice thickness 1.5–2.0 mm) for external validation. These findings suggest the framework provides accurate, generalizable sex estimation from patellar CT, supporting its potential as an objective forensic tool extendable to other skeletal sites.

title: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 Complicated by Moyamoya Syndrome with Secondary Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Objective： To analyze the clinical characteristics and pathogenesis of spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage secondary to neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)-associated moyamoya syndrome (MMS), and summarize standardized diagnosis and individualized surgical strategies for this rare comorbidity. Methods： The clinical, pathological, imaging and follow-up data of one 42-year-old female patient with NF1 combined with bilateral moyamoya syndrome and basal ganglia hemorrhage admitted in August 2025 were retrospectively collected. Relevant domestic and international literatures were systematically reviewed to summarize the clinical features and treatment principles of this disease. Results： The patient had lifelong typical NF1 cutaneous lesions without traditional cerebrovascular risk factors. Emergency CT revealed massive basal ganglia hemorrhage with mass effect and cerebral hernia risk. MRA confirmed bilateral distal internal carotid artery occlusion and typical moyamoya vascular network. Subcutaneous tumor pathology and immunohistochemistry verified benign neurofibroma. She received emergency hematoma evacuation plus decompressive craniectomy, followed by cranioplasty later. Three-month follow-up CT showed complete hematoma absorption, and the patient achieved favorable neurological recovery. Conclusion： NF1-related moyamoya syndrome should be suspected in middle-aged patients with unexplained intracerebral hemorrhage. Staged surgical management including emergency decompression and subsequent cerebral revascularization can effectively reduce the risk of recurrent stroke. Long-term multidisciplinary follow-up is required for genetic counseling and vascular monitoring.

title: Pretreatment IVIM histogram parameters using multiple ROI strategies for predicting treatment response and survival outcomes in locally advanced rectal cancer
abstract: Abstract Purpose To evaluate pretreatment intravoxel incoherent motion diffusion-weighted imaging (IVIM)-derived histogram and percentile parameters obtained using different regions of interest (ROI) delineation strategies for predicting tumor regression grade (TRG), pathological complete response (pCR) and survival outcomes in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). Materials and methods A total of 113 patients with LARC who underwent pretreatment IVIM were retrospectively enrolled. Histogram and percentile parameters of the true diffusion coefficient (D), pseudo-diffusion coefficient (D*), and perfusion fraction ( f ) were extracted using three ROI delineation strategies, including whole-tumor volume ROI (ROI WTV ), single-slice ROI (ROI SS ), and reader-defined small-sample ROI (ROI RDSS ). Patients were divided into good responders (TRG 0–1) and poor responders (TRG 2–3). Predictive models were constructed using LASSO and multivariate logistic regression. The area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) was used to evaluate the predictive performance. Survival outcomes were evaluated using Kaplan–Meier analysis. Results f _mean was incorporated into all three ROI models, while D_kurtosis was additionally included only in the ROI RDSS model. The ROI RDSS model demonstrated the best performance for predicting good responders and pCR, with AUCs of 0.883 and 0.822, respectively, outperformed the other ROI strategies. Patients in the high ROI RDSS model score had a better 3-year DFS rate than those with low scores (87.2% vs. 70.1%, p = 0.022). Conclusion Pretreatment IVIM histogram analysis may predict treatment response and survival in patients with LARC, with the ROI RDSS strategy showing the best predictive performance.

title: Photon-Counting Computed Tomography Improves Interobserver Agreement in the Evaluation of Failed Stapes Surgery
abstract: Abstract Purpose Failed stapes surgery presents a diagnostic challenge requiring high-resolution imaging to guide revision. Energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) is widely used but limited by spatial resolution and metal artifact. Photon-counting CT (PCCT) offers improved spatial resolution and reduced noise, with potential advantages in temporal bone imaging. The purpose of this study was to compare PCCT and EID-CT in identifying etiologies of failed primary stapes surgery, with emphasis on diagnostic accuracy, interobserver agreement, and interpreter confidence Methods In this retrospective study, 38 patients with failed primary stapes surgery who underwent successful revision surgery and pre-revision CT were included; 18 underwent PCCT and 20 underwent EID-CT. Three expert reviewers independently determined the cause of surgical failure, compared against the reference standard of intraoperative findings at revision. Diagnostic accuracy, interobserver agreement (Fleiss kappa), and reader confidence were compared between modalities. Results Overall interobserver agreement was substantially higher with PCCT (κ = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.60–0.90) than EID-CT (κ = 0.44; 95% CI, 0.30–0.59), with improved agreement observed across etiologies of failure; confidence intervals were non-overlapping for overall agreement and ossicular discontinuity. Consensus diagnostic accuracy was comparable between modalities (88.9% PCCT vs 85% EID-CT; p = 1.00), as was interpreter confidence (4.33 PCCT vs 4.17 EID-CT; p = 0.29). Conclusion In this small cohort, PCCT and EID-CT demonstrated similar diagnostic accuracy and reader confidence, whereas PCCT demonstrated significantly higher interobserver agreement, suggesting more reproducible assessment of failed stapes surgery and a potential role in supporting revision surgical planning.

title: Epithelioid Haemangioendothelioma of the Gastric Wall with Unique Histomorphology: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma (EHE) is an ultra-rare vascular neoplasm, characterized by local aggressiveness and metastatic potential. We report a case of primary gastric wall EHE in a 64-year-old man, detected incidentally on imaging. Case presentation: Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a well-circumscribed 18×19×14.5 mm mass arising from the gastric serosa with mild enhancement. Laparoscopic excision was performed. Histology demonstrated a heterogeneous tumour composed of cords, strands or small nests of endothelial and spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm embedded in a myxohyaline stroma. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) stain shows the neoplastic cells were negative for keratins, CD117, DOG1, S100, Desmin, HMB45, and STAT6, but diffuse positive for the endothelial marker CD34, focally positive for SMA, with a low Ki-67 proliferation index (~ 3%). The initial diagnosis was a low-grade mesenchymal neoplasm. On referral to a specialist center, additional IHC revealed strong nuclear TFE3 expression and absence of CAMTA1 and FLI1. These findings were highly suggestive of a YAP1-TFE3 rearranged epithelioid haemangioendothelioma. Although molecular confirmation was not performed in this case, the immune profile and histomorphology strongly supported this diagnosis. Conclusions This case highlights the importance of considering EHE in the differential diagnosis of gastric mesenchymal tumors and underscores the utility of TFE3 and CAMTA1 immunohistochemistry in guiding further diagnostic workup, particularly when molecular testing is unavailable.

title: Multi-view deep learning for classification of maxillary canine impaction severity using CBCT-derived images
abstract: Abstract Introduction. Accurate assessment of maxillary canine impaction is essential for timely orthodontic intervention. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a deep learning model using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) derived images to classify maxillary canine impaction severity. Methods. This retrospective study included 148 maxillary canines from 74 patients, yielding 592 CBCT-derived images across four views (panoramic, frontal cephalogram, lateral cephalogram, and cross-sectional). Images were classified into normal eruption, mild impaction, and severe impaction based on orthodontist-defined radiographic criteria. A convolutional neural network (CNN), DenseNet-121, was fine-tuned and evaluated using five-fold cross-validation. Tooth-level predictions were obtained by combining per-view outputs, and performance was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results. At the tooth level, the multi-view model achieved an overall accuracy of 91.2%, with a macro-averaged AUC of 0.94. Per-class sensitivity reached 93.4% (normal), 76.9% (mild), and 91.5% (severe); specificity exceeded 92% for all three classes. Conclusions. The proposed multi-view CNN model enables automated classification of maxillary canine impaction severity and demonstrates improved diagnostic performance with multi-view integration. This orthodontist-developed model may support early detection and multidisciplinary collaboration.

title: Extended Reality-Based Hepatic Surgical Planning: Impact on Task Time, Anatomic Accuracy, and Cognitive Burden in Novice Surgeons
abstract: Abstract Background : Traditional liver surgery education relies on 2D imaging and cadaveric specimens, causing misjudgments in complex 3D anatomy and hemodynamics, especially among junior surgeons. Objective : To develop LiverXR-Plan, a multimodal extended reality platform integrating structural imaging and hemodynamic simulation for education and surgical planning. Design : A prospective controlled trial compared LiverXR-Plan with 2D methods. Participants: 52 medical students and 47 residents. Interventions: Preoperative planning using 2D CT or LiverXR-Plan with 3D reconstruction and CFD simulation. Outcomes: Anatomical accuracy, completion time, and NASA-TLX workload. Results : Accuracy improved from 32.69% to 100% (students) and 74.47% to 100% (residents); time reduced by 54.40% and 51.12%. Hemodynamic visualization enabled risk prediction; workload significantly decreased. Conclusions : LiverXR-Plan enhances surgical planning competency and shifts liver surgery education from experience-dependent to data-driven decision-making.

title: Clinical Characteristics, Microbiological Profile, and Antimicrobial Resistance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in Hospitalized Patients with Bronchiectasis: A 10-Year Single- Center Cohort Study
abstract: Abstract Background. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is the most clinically significant respiratory pathogen in patients with bronchiectasis, yet data from mainland China on PA colonization, antimicrobial resistance, and its impact on hospitalization outcomes remain limited. We aimed to characterize the clinical and microbiological profile of PA among hospitalized patients with bronchiectasis over a 10-year period. Methods. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of all adult patients hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of bronchiectasis at Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, a tertiary referral respiratory center in China, between January 2014 and December 2024. Clinical, radiological, laboratory, and microbiological data were extracted from the electronic hospital information system. Respiratory samples were cultured using standard microbiological methods; antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by the clinical microbiology laboratory. Patients were classified as PA-positive or PA-negative on the basis of respiratory culture results. Comparisons between groups used the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with PA colonization. Results. Among 7787 hospital admissions from 2,503 unique patients (mean age 59.9 ± 13.4 years; 56.4% female), 942 admissions (29.2%) underwent respiratory culture. PA was the dominant pathogen, isolated in 338 of 942 cultured admissions (35.9%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (3.0%), Acinetobacter baumannii (2.4%), and Aspergillus spp. (6.2%). PA-positive admissions were younger (median 60 vs. 64 years), had longer hospitalization (12 vs. 11 days), higher white blood cell counts (7.28 vs. 6.56 × 10⁹/L), higher platelet counts, and higher PaCO2 (51 vs. 44 mmHg) than PA-negative admissions (all p < 0.05). In multivariable analysis, CT-documented bronchiectasis (adjusted OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.19–2.24) and higher WBC count (adjusted OR 1.06 per unit, 95% CI 1.02–1.10) were independently associated with PA colonization, whereas older age was protective (adjusted OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.97–0.99). Among 821 PA isolates with comprehensive susceptibility testing, 20.0% were multidrug-resistant, 26.4% were carbapenem-resistant, and 25.0% were fluoroquinolone-resistant; amikacin and tobramycin retained the highest susceptibility rates (90.4% and 93.8%, respectively). CT-documented bronchiectasis was also the strongest predictor of recurrent hospitalization (adjusted OR 3.17, 95% CI 2.46–4.07). Conclusions. PA is the predominant respiratory pathogen among hospitalized patients with bronchiectasis in Beijing, associated with more extensive structural lung disease, higher systemic inflammation, worse ventilatory function, and prolonged hospitalization. The substantial rates of carbapenem and fluoroquinolone resistance underscore the need for systematic surveillance and antibiotic stewardship in this population.

title: Underlying histopathology features of white matter hyperintensities in vascular and neurodegenerative disorders: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract White matter hyperintensities (WMHs) are a hallmark of cerebral small vessel disease, commonly seen in cognitively normal older adults and patients with neurodegenerative disorders, and are thought to reflect varying degrees of tissue damage. Although FLAIR and T2-weighted MRI remain the best modalities for detecting WMHs, these lesions cannot be reliably distinguished macroscopically from normal appearing white matter, so standard neuropathology protocols do not specifically consider WMH regions unless MRI guidance is available. As a result, histopathological data on WMHs from gold-standard studies remain limited relative to their clinical prevalence. This review aimed to evaluate existing evidence linking MRI-defined WMHs to their underlying histopathology in postmortem brains from patients with various neurodegenerative disorders and aging controls. After a PubMed literature search and screening of abstracts and full texts, we included 45 articles: 10 on normal aging, 16 on Alzheimer's disease, 10 on vascular dementia, and 9 on related conditions. WMHs were histopathologically characterized by myelin loss (including spongiosis), axonal rarefaction, edema, dilated perivascular spaces, gliosis, arteriolosclerosis, and venous collagenosis, all indicative of underlying white matter pathology. The findings overall suggest that WMHs are pathologically heterogeneous, varying according to their anatomical location and distribution. Disease-specific differences in regional distribution, neuroinflammation, vascular pathology, and proteinopathy further contribute to their development and clinical significance, highlighting the need to consider both diagnosis and anatomical location when interpreting the pathological substrates of WMHs.
